## Busiest Airports Analysis

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)
library(kableExtra)

# read data
url <- "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_passenger_traffic"
page <- read_html(url)
tables <- page |> html_table(fill = TRUE)

# build dataset
t2025 <- tables[[2]] |> mutate(year = 2025)
t2024 <- tables[[3]] |> mutate(year = 2024)
t2023 <- tables[[4]] |> mutate(year = 2023)
t2022 <- tables[[5]] |> mutate(year = 2022)
t2021 <- tables[[6]] |> mutate(year = 2021)

data <- bind_rows(t2025, t2024, t2023, t2022, t2021)

# clean
data <- data |>
  mutate(
    passengers = Totalpassengers |>
      gsub("\\[.*?\\]", "", x = _) |>
      gsub(",", "", x = _) |>
      as.numeric()
  )

tidy_data <- data |>
  select(Airport, year, passengers) |>
  mutate(Airport = str_trim(Airport))

# select airports
selected_airports <- c(
  "Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport",
  "Frankfurt Airport",
  "Beijing Daxing International Airport",
  "Dubai International Airport",
  "Heathrow Airport",
  "Los Angeles International Airport"
)

# table
airport_table <- tidy_data |>
  filter(Airport %in% selected_airports) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = passengers) |>
  arrange(Airport)

knitr::kable(
  airport_table,
  digits = 0,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  caption = "Passenger counts for busiest airports"
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("hold_position", "scale_down")
  ) |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(1, width = "6cm")
```

```{r fig.cap="Passenger traffic trends for selected busiest airports.", fig.width=12, fig.height=7}
#plot
plot_data <- tidy_data |>
  filter(Airport %in% selected_airports)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = year, y = passengers, color = Airport)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Passenger Traffic for Busiest Airports",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Passengers",
    color = "Airport"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  theme_minimal()
```


The table and graph show how passenger traffic changes from 2020 to 2025 for several airports. Most airports increase over time, mostly because travel increased after COVID-19. Atlanta International Airport has the highest passenger numbers and stays consistent each year. Dubai and Heathrow also show strong growth. Some airports, like Beijing and Frankfurt are missing certain years or have lower values, which shows they were not always in the top rankings. The graph helps show trends over time, while the table gives exact numbers for comparison.

## Monte Carlo Numerical Integration
```{r}
library(tidyverse)

# chi-square function
f <- function(x) {
  dchisq(x, df = 5)
}

# resolutions
n_values <- c(10, 100, 500, 1000)

results <- map_dfr(n_values, function(n) {
  
  # get points
  x <- runif(n, 0, 20)
  y <- runif(n, 0, 0.16)
  
  # classify
  under <- y <= f(x)
  
  tibble(
    x = x,
    y = y,
    under = under,
    n = n
  )
})
```

```{r fig.cap="Monte Carlo approximation of the Chi-square distribution (df = 5).", fig.width=12, fig.height=7}
# plot
ggplot(results, aes(x = x, y = y, color = under)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_function(fun = f, color = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ n) +
  labs(
    title = "Monte Carlo Approximation of Chi-square Distribution (df = 5)",
    x = "x",
    y = "y",
    color = "Under Curve"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Monte Carlo integration estimates the area under a curve by generating random points and checking whether they fall below the curve. The proportion of points under the curve is used to estimate the integral. In this case, the function is a Chi-square probability density function, so the exact value of the integral is 1. The small multiple shows that as the number of points increases, the estimate becomes more accurate. With fewer points, the estimate is rough, but with more points the values stabilize. This supports that the estimate is approaching 1.

## Planning and Prompting GenAI Tools

### Plan
**Goal:**  
The goal is to clean and organize the calcium dataset so that changes in ulnar calcium measurements can be clearly analyzed over time. Then, I will create a visualization that shows how calcium levels differ across time and between the two treatment groups.

**Verbs and Nouns Needed:**  
Nouns: computer with r installed on it, dataset, variables, calcium levels, groups, plot, graph
Verbs: load, clean, filter, select, check, inspect, tidy, create, adjust, make
  

**Steps:**  

1. Make a plan. 
2. Load the calcium dataset into R.  
3. Inspect the dataset to understand the variables.
4. Check for missing or incorrect values and clean the data.  
5. Ensure that variables are in the correct format. 
6. Select the relevant variables.  
7. Make sure that the dataset is in tidy format, where each row represents a single observation.  
8. Create a visualization using ggplot2.  
9. Check the plot to ensure it clearly shows differences between treatment groups over time.  
10. Adjust labels, scales, or formatting to improve clarity and interpretation of the graph.

### Comparison of Plan-Based vs Generic Prompting

The plan-informed response, the generic response, and my own work show clear differences in both the visualization and the overall understanding of the problem. The generic response creates a plot of average values by column, but it does not show the structure of the dataset or the goal of comparing treatment groups over time, making it uninformative for this context. In contrast, the plan-informed response produces a line graph that shows the correct structure and style the graph should have, but does not reflect the actual dataset. My own work focuses on organizing the data into a tidy format and visualizing changes over time, which helps show patterns more clearly. This comparison shows that having a clear plan leads to more accurate and useful outputs from genAI tools, while generic prompts can miss important points of the data. Overall, this shows that genAI tools are most effective when given structured guidance, but the strongest and most effective results still come from careful and independent work.


## Reflection
Throughout this semester, I have learned how to approach data analysis in a more structured and intentional way. One of the most important skills I developed is learning how to plan before coding. For exmaple, in each assignment, we first create a plan that includes a clear goal, the verbs and nouns needed, and a list of steps to take. This has helped me break down complex problems into smaller, manageable parts and made my code more organized and effective.
I have also become more comfortable working with tidy data and using tools like ggplot2 to create clear graphs. Earlier in the semester, I focused mainly on just producing the output, but now I think more about whether the visualization actually communicates the intended message.
Additionally, I learned how to use Quarto to combine code, results, and explanations into one reproducible document. This will improve how I present my work and it will make it easier to follow. Overall, this course has helped me build strong skills not only in coding, but also in planning, organizing, and clearly communicating data analysis.
